items.title: Dick Katz interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002
items.q: I think Bird was playing it.

ctx.x: There’s something in the water in Detroit. I’m convinced. Because all these guys had the same thing. I called it, it was their version of Charlie Parker, it was this line, this lyrical line that they all knew how to play, like Pepper Adams, Tommy Flanagan, Barry Harris, Billy Mitchell, who wasn’t really from Detroit but he wound up there, Paul Chambers, Kenny Burrell, I’m probably leaving out some. Roland was a little bit different, Roland Hanna. Because he was basically classical pianist that switched to jazz on…

items.title: Dick Katz interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002
items.q: Of course the folklore, I mean the Charlie Parkers of the world were larger than life people.

ctx.x: But back in the twenties, you know Louis sang about it, pot, gage, whatever they called it that marijuana was — but that, the alcoholism wasn’t peculiar to musicians and the musicians didn’t get the rap of, I think big time — for instance like the white bands and the colored bands that were really, the black bands, colored, Jimmie Lunceford and those bands, particularly bands like Jimmie Lunceford and to a lesser extent Basie, even though these guys were free spirits, the discipline in the bands was considerable.…

fixed it so they would fire themselves, which is a great lesson in — when you have self esteem to that level — Basie was great, he was quietly running that band but he knew what was going on. So to the alcoholism you’re talking about the ones where it impacted to the point where it was messing them up would be like any other profession, you drink yourself out of a job.
